description:
Team Name: Kingdom of Sophos

About Us: 10th graders at METU H.S. in Ankara with a passion for software, physics, and space exploration. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we're building an immersive astronaut mission trainer turning space engineering trade-offs into an interactive learning experience.

Team Status: Selective / By Invitation

Policy: If you have achievements in physics, math, or coding, contact us. Requirements: Fluent English & Turkish, 80+ GPA.
summary:
Red Horizons (by Kingdom of Sophos) is a first-person Mars survival and science game for children aged 7–10, built in Unity. Players land on Mars by rocket and build their outpost by hand: they carry equipment, choose sites (an icy crater for the ice drill, a sunny ridge for solar panels), lay power cables and keep oxygen, water, energy and food in balance. They also eat, sleep and shelter from storms. Every morning, Mission Control gives a briefing based on real solar flare records from NASA’s DONKI space weather database, so players learn to prepare for radiation and dust storms.

For the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, Red Horizons teaches the scientific method instead of using quizzes. Players form a hypothesis, choose a fair experiment design, take measurements by hand, analyze the data and file a report. If a design is flawed, Mission Control explains why after the first result.

The game turns abstract space facts into lived experience. Children learn systems thinking, resource management and data-driven decision making, the skills future astronauts need. Our message: every decision has a consequence.
details: Red Horizons is a first-person Mars survival and science game for children aged 7–10, built for the "Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. The player lands on Mars as a commander, gets a daily briefing from Mission Control based on real NASA data, carries supplies, builds a solar array and base by hand, and runs real science experiments in the lab (like splitting water into oxygen and hydrogen) by choosing an experiment design and taking measurements. Real space-weather history from NASA DONKI drives events such as dust storms that drain power, so every decision has a consequence. Instead of quizzes, children learn by doing: energy, resource management, the scientific method and Mars facts (e.g., gravity is 38% of Earth's). Tools: Unity 6 (URP), C#, Blender/Meshy for 3D models, ffmpeg for video. Our team designed it to be safe, ad-free and playable in a web browser.
